components.note: 石 (stone, mineral) — 矾 names a mineral salt, alum.
凡 (fán) gives the sound — an exact match with 矾's reading.

example.pinyin: Gōngrén wǎng shuǐ lǐ jiā le míngfán.
example.english: The workers added alum to the water.
example.fact: Alum has been used for thousands of years to purify drinking water — it makes suspended dirt particles clump together and sink, a process called flocculation.

components.note: 石 (stone, mineral) — 硼 names boron, an element found in borate minerals.
朋 (péng) gives the sound — an exact match with 硼's reading.

example.pinyin: Péngsuān kěyǐ yònglái xiāodú.
example.english: Boric acid can be used for disinfecting.
example.fact: Boron is added to ordinary glass to make borosilicate glass, such as Pyrex, which resists cracking under sudden temperature changes far better than regular glass.

components.note: 囗 (an enclosure) — 囿 originally named a walled royal hunting park or garden, later extending to 'to confine, to limit.'
有 (yǒu) is close to the sound of 囿 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā bèi jiù de sīxiǎng suǒ yòu.
example.english: He is confined by old ways of thinking.
example.fact: 囿 originally named the walled hunting parks and gardens kept by Chinese kings in antiquity — its 'enclosure' radical 囗 still pictures those walls today.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泅 describes moving through water, to swim.
囚 (qiú) gives the sound — an exact match with 泅's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā qiúshuǐ dùguò le xiǎo hé.
example.english: He swam across the small river.
example.fact: 泅 is a literary word for swimming that has largely been replaced by 游泳 in everyday Mandarin — a small example of how classical single-character verbs gave way to modern two-character compounds.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, to move) — 邂 describes an encounter that happens while out and about.
解 (xiè) gives the sound — an exact match with 邂's reading.

example.pinyin: Tāmen zài shūdiàn lǐ xièhòu le.
example.english: They ran into each other by chance in the bookstore.
example.fact: 邂 almost never appears alone — like many Chinese characters, it exists mainly as half of a single fixed word, 邂逅 (xièhòu, 'a chance encounter').

meanings: used in personal names and place names

components.note: 金 (metal) — 钜 originally described a kind of hard, high-quality iron, later used as a literary variant of 巨 ('huge').
巨 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match with 钜's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā juān chū le yì bǐ jùkuǎn.
example.english: He donated a huge sum of money.
example.fact: 钜 is a literary variant of 巨 ('huge') that keeps the metal radical 钅 because it originally described a particularly hard grade of iron in ancient Chinese texts.

meanings: insect that eats into books, clothing etc

components.note: 虫 (insect), doubled inside the character — 蠹 names an insect that bores into and eats stored books, grain, or cloth.
橐 (tuó) no longer closely resembles 蠹's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 这本古书被蠹虫咬坏了。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn gǔshū bèi dùchóng yǎo huài le.
example.english: This old book was damaged by bookworms.
example.fact: 蠹 is one of the most complex common characters, at 24 strokes — its shape literally packs two insect radicals 虫虫 under a sack 橐, picturing insects devouring something in storage.

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 垩 names a soft white clay or lime used to whitewash walls.
亚 (yà) no longer closely resembles 垩's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Gōngrén yòng shí'è fěnshuā le qiáng.
example.english: The workers whitewashed the wall with lime.
example.fact: 垩 refers to a soft, chalky white clay that was used to whitewash walls in ancient China, much like lime plaster was used across the ancient Mediterranean world.

components.note: 占 (to divine, to consult an oracle) — 乩 relates to fortune-telling and spirit mediums.
乚 does not carry a well-attested independent reading, so the phonetic link to 乩 (jī) is unclear despite being traditionally analyzed as the sound-bearing part.

example.pinyin: Lǎorén qù miào lǐ qiú jī wènbǔ.
example.english: The old man went to the temple to seek a divination.
example.fact: 乩童 (jītóng), literally 'divination child,' refers to a spirit medium in Chinese folk religion believed to channel deities — a practice still performed at temples in Taiwan today.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗝 names a sound made with the mouth, a hiccup or belch.
鬲 (gé) gives the sound — an exact match with 嗝's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā dǎ le yí gè gé.
example.english: He let out a hiccup.
example.fact: Both English 'hiccup' and Chinese 嗝 are shaped by the sound they describe — the mouth radical 口 in 嗝 marks it as one of many Chinese characters built specifically to represent noises the body makes.

meanings: historically, the name of a river in Jiangxi

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淦 originally described water seeping into the bottom of a boat.
金 (jīn) no longer closely resembles 淦's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Chuán dǐ jiànjiàn gàn le shuǐ.
example.english: Water gradually seeped into the bottom of the boat.
example.fact: In classical Chinese, 淦 was a specific nautical term for water leaking into the hull of a boat — a narrower meaning than ordinary words for 'to leak.'

etymologyHint: A hand 寸 raising a wooden 木 wine jar 酉; 尊 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 樽 as a drinking vessel or goblet made of wood, distinguishing it from cups of bronze, jade, or pottery.
尊 shares its exact sound with 樽 and was itself an ancient word for a ceremonial wine vessel — a picture of two hands presenting a jar — before it broadened to mean 'honored, respected.'

example.hanzi: 他举起酒樽向客人敬酒。
example.pinyin: Tā jǔqǐ jiǔzūn xiàng kèrén jìngjiǔ.
example.english: He raised the wine goblet to toast his guests.
example.fact: The wine vessel named by 樽 appears throughout classical Chinese poetry as a symbol of friendship and celebration, most famously in verses by the Tang-dynasty poet Li Bai.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 诮 describes a verbal act, to mock or blame.
肖 (xiāo) is close to the sound of 诮, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他常常诮骂自己的同事。
example.pinyin: Tā chángcháng qiàomà zìjǐ de tóngshì.
example.english: He often mocks and scolds his colleagues.
example.fact: 诮 survives today almost only in the compound 冷嘲热讽-adjacent literary usage and in the classical term 诮让 (to reproach) — it dropped out of everyday spoken Mandarin centuries ago.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揆 relates to handling or managing affairs, as a minister does.
癸 (guǐ) is close to the sound of 揆, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他反复揆度这件事的后果。
example.pinyin: Tā fǎnfù kuíduó zhè jiàn shì de hòuguǒ.
example.english: He repeatedly weighed the consequences of this matter.
example.fact: In imperial China, 揆 was used as a title for the prime minister — 首揆 (shǒukuí) literally meant 'chief reckoner,' the official who weighed and managed state affairs.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 啐 describes an action of the mouth, to spit or to taste.
卒 (zú) is close to the sound of 啐, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā cuì le yì kǒu tuòmo.
example.english: He spat out a mouthful of saliva.
example.fact: 啐 is built from 口 (mouth) plus 卒, and is used to write both the action of spitting and the sharp exclamation 'pshaw!' — a rare character that covers both a sound and an action of the mouth.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淅 names water used for washing rice.
析 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 淅's reading.

example.pinyin: Nǎinai yòng xǐmǐ shuǐ xǐ wǎn.
example.english: Grandma washed the dishes with rice-rinsing water.
example.fact: 淅 specifically names the water used to rinse rice before cooking — a level of specificity common in classical Chinese, which often had distinct single characters for very narrow, everyday actions.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 榉 names a type of elm tree.
举 (jǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 榉's reading.

example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ zhòng zhe yì kē jǔshù.
example.english: There is a zelkova elm tree growing in the courtyard.
example.fact: 榉 names the zelkova, a relative of the elm prized in East Asia for its hard, fine-grained wood, which is traditionally used to make furniture and bonsai.

components.note: 首 (head) — 馗 names the cheekbone, a part of the head.
九 (jiǔ) no longer closely resembles 馗's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo lùkǒu jiàozuò kuí jiē.
example.english: This intersection is called Kui Street.
example.fact: 馗 originally meant a major crossroads or thoroughfare in classical Chinese, a sense mostly preserved today only in place names and the mythological figure Zhong Kui (钟馗), a demon-quelling deity.

etymologyHint: Rope 纟 yoking a horse to a chariot 车 by its mouth 口

components.note: 纟 (silk, rope), shown twice in the full form, names the reins — ropes used to guide a horse.
车 (a cart or chariot) combines with 口 (mouth, the bit in the horse's mouth) to complete the picture: rope reins running from a rider's hands, through the horse's mouth, to the chariot it pulls.

example.pinyin: Qíshǒu lā jǐn le mǎ de pèitou.
example.english: The rider pulled the horse's reins tight.
example.fact: 辔 survives mainly in the classical phrase 并驾齐驱 (side by side, at the same pace) and in the idiom 悬崖勒马 (to rein in the horse at the cliff's edge, meaning to stop before disaster) — both drawn from the old imagery of controlling a horse by its reins.

etymologyHint: The sun 日 moving 辶; 隹 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 日 (sun) combined with 辶 (to walk, to move) pictures the sun advancing across the sky, giving 暹 its meaning 'to rise, to advance.'
隹 (zhuī, a short-tailed bird) does not closely match 暹's modern sound (xiān); any phonetic connection has drifted apart over time, though it is traditionally treated as the sound-bearing part.

example.hanzi: 太阳渐渐暹升到天空中。
example.pinyin: Tàiyáng jiànjiàn xiān shēng dào tiānkōng zhōng.
example.english: The sun gradually rose into the sky.
example.fact: 暹 is the character used to transliterate 'Siam,' the historical name for Thailand — 暹罗 (Xiānluó) was the standard Chinese name for the Siamese kingdom for centuries.

etymologyHint: A horse 马 working hard 敄; 敄 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骛 describes a horse galloping or rushing about.
敄 (wù) shares 骛's exact sound; it depicts exertion or striving, reinforcing the sense of a horse straining forward at a gallop.

example.pinyin: Nà pǐ mǎ wùchí zài cǎoyuán shàng.
example.english: That horse galloped across the grassland.
example.fact: 骛 survives today mainly in the idiom 好高骛远 (hào gāo wù yuǎn, 'to reach high and aim far'), a warning against setting unrealistic, overambitious goals.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鱿 names the squid, a sea creature classed with fish in the traditional radical system.
尤 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 鱿's reading.

example.pinyin: Māma mǎi le yìxiē yóuyú.
example.english: Mom bought some squid.
example.fact: 鱿鱼 (yóuyú, 'squid') is a favorite Chinese street food, often grilled on skewers — and the phrase 炒鱿鱼 ('to fry squid') is Cantonese-derived slang for firing someone from a job, since a squid curls up when cooked much like a bedroll being rolled up to leave.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苫 names a mat woven from rushes or straw.
占 (zhàn) is close to the sound of 苫, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wūdǐng shàng gài zhe yì céng shān.
example.english: The roof is covered with a layer of straw matting.
example.fact: 苫 names woven straw or reed matting once widely used to thatch roofs and cover goods in traditional China, before being displaced by tile, metal, and plastic sheeting.

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 犷 describes wild, uncivilized behavior, as of an untamed animal.
广 (guǎng) gives the sound — an exact match with 犷's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī láng kànqǐlái hěn guǎngyě.
example.english: This wolf looks very wild and fierce.
example.fact: 犷 appears almost exclusively in the compound 犷野 or 粗犷 (cūguǎng, 'rough and bold'), a word often used approvingly today to describe a rugged, unpolished style in art or manner.

meanings: to hunt at night by torches
etymologyHint: Hunting with dogs 犭 and torches 尞; 尞 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) ties 獠 to hunting with animals.
尞 (liào) is close to the sound of 獠 (liáo) — the same syllable, just a different tone — and originally depicted a torch or bonfire, evoking night hunts by firelight.

example.hanzi: 古时猎人常常獠猎夜行的野兽。
example.pinyin: Gǔshí lièrén chángcháng liáoliè yèxíng de yěshòu.
example.english: In ancient times, hunters often hunted nocturnal animals by torchlight.
example.fact: 獠 originally described hunting at night using torches to spot and drive game — a practice recorded in ancient Chinese hunting texts long before firearms existed.

etymologyHint: To implicate 罒 someone by one's words 言

components.note: 罒 suggests entangling or trapping someone, an image of accusation.
言 (words, speech) shows 詈 is about verbal attack — combined with 罒, the image is of catching someone with cutting words, hence 'to scold, to curse.'

example.pinyin: Tā bù gāi nàyàng lìmà háizi.
example.english: He shouldn't scold the child like that.
example.fact: 詈 pairs with 骂 in the compound 詈骂 (to curse, to revile) — both characters independently mean 'to scold,' a common pattern in Chinese where two near-synonyms are joined into one stronger word.

components.note: 立 (to stand) reflects 竦's meaning of standing up straight or rigid, whether from awe, reverence, or fear.
束 (to bind, to restrain) suggests a body tensed and drawn tight, as when someone stiffens with fear or respect, giving 竦 its sense 'to be in awe, to shudder.'

example.hanzi: 大家对他的勇气竦然起敬。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì tā de yǒngqì sǒngrán qǐjìng.
example.english: Everyone was struck with awe and respect for his courage.
example.fact: 竦 shares its root sense of 'to raise up, to stand alert' with the more common character 悚 (sǒng, 'terrified'), which replaced it in most modern words for fear, such as 毛骨悚然 (a chill down one's spine).

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 篙 names a bamboo pole used to punt a boat.
高 (gāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 篙's reading.

example.pinyin: Chuánfū yòng zhú gāo chēng chuán.
example.english: The boatman punts the boat with a bamboo pole.
example.fact: 撑竿跳 (pole vaulting) and river punting both rely on a long pole for leverage — 篙 specifically names the pole used by boatmen to push off the riverbed or bank.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 诨 names a joking, ribald remark.
军 (jūn) is close to the sound of 诨, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan kāi hùn wánxiào.
example.english: He likes to crack jokes and banter.
example.fact: 诨 appears in 打诨 (dǎhùn, 'to crack jokes'), a term from traditional Chinese theater describing the comic asides a clown-role actor would use to lighten the mood between serious scenes.

etymologyHint: Objects with a metal 钅 joint 交; 交 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 铰 as a metal implement, such as a pair of scissors or a hinge.
交 (jiāo, 'to cross, to join') is close to the sound of 铰 (jiǎo) — the same syllable, different tone — and pictures two blades crossing, as in scissors, or two metal pieces joined at a hinge.

example.pinyin: Lǐfàshī yòng jiǎodāo jiǎn tóufa.
example.english: The barber cuts hair with shears.
example.fact: 铰 gives its name to 铰链 (jiǎoliàn, 'hinge'), the everyday word for the metal joint that lets a door swing — the same character also names scissors, since both a hinge and a pair of scissors work by two parts pivoting together.

meanings: used in 餛飩|馄饨[hun2 tun5] and 餛燉|馄炖[hun2 dun4]

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馄 names a food, as in 馄饨 (húntun, wonton soup).
昆 (kūn) is close to the sound of 馄, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen qù chī le yì wǎn húntun.
example.english: We went and ate a bowl of wonton soup.
example.fact: 馄饨 (húntun) shares its Old Chinese root with 混沌 (hùndùn, 'primordial chaos') — folk etymology links the dumpling's shapeless wrapped filling to the formless chaos said to exist before the world took shape.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蜚 names the cockroach.
非 (fēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜚's reading.

example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ yǒu yì zhī fěilián.
example.english: There is a cockroach in the kitchen.
example.fact: 蜚蠊 (fěilián) is the formal, scientific name for the cockroach in Chinese, while 蟑螂 (zhāngláng) is the everyday word — much like 'blattodean' versus 'cockroach' in English.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峒 names a mountain or a cave.
同 (tóng) is close to the sound of 峒, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shānqū lǐ yǒu hěn duō dòngxué.
example.english: There are many mountain caves in this hilly area.
example.fact: 峒 appears in the names of several mountains and cave systems across China, including Kongtong Mountain (崆峒山) in Gansu, a site sacred to Taoism.

etymologyHint: A sparkling 莹 lake 氵; 莹 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 滢 as a description of water — clear and pure.
莹 shares 滢's exact sound (yíng) and itself means 'lustrous, glittering like jade,' lending 滢 its sense of water that is clear and sparkling.

example.pinyin: Húshuǐ qīngyíng jiàndǐ.
example.english: The lake water is so clear you can see the bottom.
example.fact: 滢 is built from 氵 (water) plus 莹 ('lustrous, like jade'), a combination that shows up almost exclusively in given names, where parents choose it to suggest clarity and purity.

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 琬 names a piece of fine jade.
宛 (wǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 琬's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā pèidài zhe yí kuài wǎnyù.
example.english: She wears a piece of fine jade.
example.fact: 琬 names a rounded, symmetrical piece of ceremonial jade once carried by nobles in ancient China as a symbol of virtue and rank.

components.note: 见 (to see) — 靓 relates to appearance — to make up one's face so as to look attractive.
青 (qīng) is close to the sound of 靓, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā duì zhe jìngzi jìngzhuāng.
example.english: She put on her makeup in front of the mirror.
example.fact: 靓 is pronounced jìng in the classical sense 'to make up one's face,' but as liàng it is common Cantonese-influenced slang for 'pretty' or 'handsome,' as in 靓仔 (liàngzái, 'handsome guy') — the same character carries two quite different readings and registers.

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 狻 names a legendary lion-like beast, as in 狻猊.
夋 (qūn) no longer closely resembles the sound of 狻 (suān) — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it is traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 石狮子的造型来自传说中的狻猊。
example.pinyin: Shí shīzi de zàoxíng láizì chuánshuō zhōng de suānní.
example.english: The stone lion's design comes from the legendary suanni beast.
example.fact: 狻猊 (suānní) is one of nine mythical dragon-children in Chinese folklore, said to resemble a lion and to enjoy sitting still — which is why its image decorates the bases of incense burners and Buddhist thrones.

etymologyHint: The luster 粲 of a gem 王; 粲 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade, when used at the left of a character) ties 璨 to gems and precious stones.
粲 shares 璨's exact sound (càn) and means 'bright, resplendent,' giving 璨 its meaning 'the brilliant luster of a gem.'

example.pinyin: Tā de xiàngliàn cuǐcàn duómù.
example.english: Her necklace sparkles dazzlingly.
example.fact: 璀璨 (cuǐcàn) is a rare case where both characters are built the same way, each pairing 王 (jade) with a phonetic that means 'bright' — the whole word describes the brilliant luster of gemstones.

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 犟 describes stubbornness, as an ox digging in its heels.
强 (jiàng) gives the sound — an exact match with 犟's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè tóu niú hěn jiàng, bùkěn zǒu.
example.english: This ox is very stubborn and refuses to walk.
example.fact: 犟 is built by simply stacking 强 (strong) over 牛 (ox) — a straightforward visual pun for 'as stubborn as an ox,' an image just as common in Chinese as it is in English.

meanings: used in 鸕鶿|鸬鹚[lu2 ci2]

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸬 names the cormorant, a fishing bird.
卢 (lú) gives the sound — an exact match with 鸬's reading.

example.pinyin: Yúmín yòng lúcí bǔ yú.
example.english: Fishermen use cormorants to catch fish.
example.fact: For centuries, fishermen along China's rivers, especially in Guilin, have trained cormorants (鸬鹚) to dive and catch fish, sometimes with a loose ring around the bird's throat so it cannot swallow the larger catch.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 螨 names the mite, a tiny insect-like creature.
㒼 (mǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 螨's reading; it is the same phonetic element found in 满/滿 (mǎn, "full").

example.pinyin: Chǒngwù shēnshang fāxiàn le mǎnchóng.
example.english: Mites were found on the pet's body.
example.fact: Dust mites (螨) are too small to see with the naked eye, yet they are one of the most common triggers of indoor allergies and asthma worldwide.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 芩 names a marsh plant.
今 (jīn) is close to the sound of 芩, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Huángqín shì yì zhǒng zhōngyào cái.
example.english: Huangqin is a type of Chinese medicinal herb.
example.fact: 黄芩 (huángqín) is a root used in traditional Chinese medicine that modern research has confirmed contains baicalin, a compound studied for its anti-inflammatory properties.

meanings: used in 嘹亮[liao2 liang4] and 嘹喨[liao2 liang4]

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嘹 describes a sound made vocally, a clear resonant tone.
尞 (liào) is close to the sound of 嘹 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Yuǎnchù chuánlái liáoliàng de gēshēng.
example.english: A clear, resonant song carried over from the distance.
example.fact: 嘹亮 (liáoliàng) describes a sound that is both loud and clear, and is the standard word used in Chinese to praise a singer's or trumpet's ringing tone.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锟 names a legendary sword forged of fine steel.
昆 (kūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 锟's reading.

example.hanzi: 传说中的锟铻剑削玉如泥。
example.pinyin: Chuánshuō zhōng de kūnwú jiàn xiāo yù rú ní.
example.english: The legendary Kunwu sword could cut jade like mud.
example.fact: 锟铻 is named in the ancient text Liezi as a sword of extraordinary sharpness, said in legend to slice through jade as easily as mud.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蜇 names the jellyfish, traditionally classed with insects and small creatures.
折 (zhē) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜇's reading.

example.hanzi: 海边的人被水蜇刺伤了。
example.pinyin: Hǎibiān de rén bèi shuǐzhē cì shāng le.
example.english: The person at the seaside was stung by a jellyfish.
example.fact: 水蜇 (shuǐzhē) is a common Chinese name for jellyfish, and dried, salted jellyfish (海蜇, hǎizhé) is a classic cold appetizer in Chinese cuisine, prized for its crunchy texture.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洹 names a river in Henan province.
亘 (gèn) no longer closely resembles 洹's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Huán shuǐ liújīng Hénán Ānyáng.
example.english: The Huan River flows through Anyang, Henan.
example.fact: The Huan River (洹水) runs past Anyang, the site of the ancient Shang dynasty capital where the earliest known Chinese writing, oracle bone script, was excavated in the early twentieth century.

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 comb 节; 节 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) reflects that a comb (栉) was traditionally carved from wood or bamboo.
节 (jié) no longer closely resembles the modern sound of 栉 (zhì); any phonetic link has drifted apart over time, though a comb's regularly spaced teeth do echo the segments 节 depicts.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng mù zhì shūlǐ tóufa.
example.english: She combs her hair with a wooden comb.
example.fact: 栉 survives today mainly in the idiom 栉风沐雨 (zhìfēng mùyǔ, 'combed by wind, bathed by rain'), a vivid image for enduring hardship while traveling or working outdoors.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俪 relates to a paired couple, husband and wife.
丽 (lì) gives the sound — an exact match with 俪's reading.

example.pinyin: Tāmen shì yí duì kànglì.
example.english: They are a married couple.
example.fact: 伉俪 (kànglì) is a formal, respectful word for 'husband and wife' still used today in wedding speeches and obituaries, even though neither character appears in ordinary daily vocabulary.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钍 names thorium, a metallic element.
土 (tǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 钍's reading.

example.pinyin: Tǔ shì yì zhǒng fàngshèxìng jīnshǔ.
example.english: Thorium is a radioactive metal.
example.fact: Thorium (钍) is being researched as a potential nuclear fuel because it is roughly three to four times more abundant in the Earth's crust than uranium.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锨 names a metal-bladed shovel.
欣 (xīn) is close to the sound of 锨, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Gōngrén yòng xiān wā tǔ.
example.english: The worker digs soil with a shovel.
example.fact: 锨 specifically names a shovel with a flat, broad blade for digging or scooping loose material, distinct from 铁锹 (also 'shovel'), with which it is largely interchangeable in modern usage.

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 瑁 names a fine piece of jade.
冒 (mào) gives the sound — an exact match with 瑁's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè kuài mào yù diāokè jīngměi.
example.english: This piece of fine jade is exquisitely carved.
example.fact: 瑁 also names a type of sea turtle shell prized as an ornament in classical China, sharing its character with 玳瑁 (dàimào, 'tortoiseshell'), the material still used today in decorative inlays.

components.note: 豆 (originally a ritual offering vessel) sits at the base of 壹; the character's oldest sense was 'uniform, wholly one,' which made it a natural formal stand-in for the numeral 一 (one) on checks and legal documents, since it is far harder to alter or forge than a simple stroke.

example.pinyin: Zhīpiào shàng yào xiě yī bǎi yuán zhěng.
example.english: The check should be written as exactly one hundred yuan.
example.fact: 壹, 贰, and 叁 are the formal "banker's" numerals for one, two, and three used on checks and contracts in China precisely because they are much harder to alter with an extra stroke than the simple 一, 二, 三.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痿 names a condition of the body, paralysis or atrophy.
委 (wěi) gives the sound — an exact match with 痿's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā yīn bìng wěi le shuāng tuǐ.
example.english: His legs became paralyzed due to illness.
example.fact: 痿 appears in 阳痿 (yángwěi), the standard clinical term in Chinese for erectile dysfunction, and in 脑血栓引起的痿症, describing paralysis or muscle wasting from illness.

example.pinyin: Zhè piàn tiándì hóng dà wú biān.
example.english: This field is vast and boundless.
example.fact: 竑 is an extremely rare literary character today, surviving mainly as a component for describing vastness in classical Chinese texts and occasionally in given names.

components.note: 米 (rice, grain) — 粕 names the leftover grains and dregs from distilling liquor.
白 (bái) no longer closely resembles 粕's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Jiǔzāo de kāngpò bèi rēngdiào le.
example.english: The dregs from the wine mash were thrown away.
example.fact: 糟粕 (zāopò) literally names the leftover dregs from brewing or distilling, but the word is used figuratively in Chinese to mean 'worthless remnants,' as in the phrase 取其精华，去其糟粕 ('take the essence, discard the dross').

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 犄 names an ox's horn.
奇 (jī) gives the sound — an exact match with 犄's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī niú de jījiǎo hěn cháng.
example.english: This cow's horn is very long.
example.fact: 犄角 (jījiǎo) means both 'an animal's horn' and, by extension, 'a corner or nook' — as in 犄角旮旯 (jījiǎo gālá), a colloquial phrase for every last hidden corner of a place.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 瘙 names a skin condition, itching.
蚤 (zǎo) is close to the sound of 瘙, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Pífū sàoyǎng de ràng rén nánshòu.
example.english: The itchy skin is really uncomfortable.
example.fact: 瘙痒 (sàoyǎng) is the standard medical term in Chinese for itching, and appears on the packaging of most anti-itch creams and lotions sold in China.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饯 relates to food, as in a farewell dinner or preserved fruit.
戋 (jiān) is close to the sound of 饯 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Péngyoumen wèi tā jiànxíng.
example.english: Friends held a farewell dinner for him.
example.fact: 饯行 (jiànxíng), 'to see someone off with a meal,' preserves a custom recorded as far back as the Zhou dynasty, when travelers were given a ritual send-off banquet before a long journey.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抟 describes an action of the hand, to roll something round.
专 (zhuān) is close to the sound of 抟, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ miàntuán tuán chéng le qiúzhuàng.
example.english: He rolled the dough into a ball shape.
example.fact: 抟 appears in the classical idiom 抟沙作糕 ('molding sand into a cake'), used to describe an effort that looks purposeful but is doomed to fall apart, since sand cannot truly be shaped and held together.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 衲 describes an action done to cloth, to mend or patch a garment.
内 (nèi) is close to the sound of 衲, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Lǎo sēng chuān zhe yí jiàn bǎinàyī.
example.english: The old monk wears a robe patched together from many pieces.
example.fact: 百衲衣 (bǎinàyī), 'the robe of a hundred patches,' was traditionally worn by Buddhist monks who took a vow of poverty, stitching their robe together from donated scraps of cloth rather than buying new fabric.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踮 describes an action of the foot, to stand on tiptoe.
店 (diàn) is close to the sound of 踮 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā diǎn qǐ jiǎojiān qù ná shū.
example.english: She stood on tiptoe to reach for the book.
example.fact: 踮脚 (diǎnjiǎo), 'to stand on tiptoe,' is the same motion ballet dancers use en pointe — though in Chinese the word is just as often used for the everyday act of reaching a high shelf.

meanings: (of a bucktooth) to protrude; to stick out

components.note: 齿 (teeth) — 龅 describes teeth that protrude, a bucktooth.
包 (bāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 龅's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā de ményá yǒudiǎn bāo.
example.english: His front teeth stick out a little.
example.fact: 龅牙 (bāoyá), 'buck teeth,' combines the teeth radical 齿 with 包 ('to wrap, to bulge'), a straightforward visual description of teeth that protrude outward.

etymologyHint: To persist 复 in error 忄; 复 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) ties 愎 to an attitude or disposition — here, an unyielding one.
复 (fù, 'to repeat, to return to') no longer closely resembles 愎's sound (bì), but the idea of returning again and again to the same course reinforces 愎's meaning 'stubborn, unwilling to change.'

example.pinyin: Tā gùzhí yòu gāngbì zìyòng.
example.english: He is stubborn and self-opinionated.
example.fact: 刚愎自用 (gāngbì zìyòng), 'stubborn and self-important,' is a fixed four-character idiom that appears in the ancient historical text Zuo Zhuan, describing rulers who refuse to listen to advice.

components.note: 香 (fragrant) — 馥 names a rich fragrance or scent.
复 (fù) gives the sound — an exact match with 馥's reading.

example.hanzi: 屋子里弥漫着馥郁的香气。
example.pinyin: Wūzi lǐ mímàn zhe fùyù de xiāngqì.
example.english: The room is filled with a rich, fragrant smell.
example.fact: 馥郁 (fùyù) describes a fragrance so strong it seems to fill the air, and is the standard word Chinese perfume and tea packaging uses to advertise a rich, lingering scent.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 梏 names wooden handcuffs or fetters.
告 (gào) is close to the sound of 梏, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Fànrén de shǒu shàng dài zhe gù.
example.english: The prisoner's hands are bound with wooden handcuffs.
example.fact: 桎梏 (zhìgù), meaning ankle shackles and wrist manacles together, is used figuratively in modern Chinese to mean any oppressive restriction, as in 封建礼教的桎梏 ('the shackles of feudal moral codes').

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 讣 names a spoken or written announcement of a death, an obituary.
卜 (bǔ) is close to the sound of 讣, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Jiārén shōudào le fùgào.
example.english: The family received the obituary notice.
example.fact: 讣告 (fùgào) is the standard formal term in Chinese for a published obituary or death notice, still used today in newspapers and on funeral programs.

components.note: 阝 (place, settlement) — 邝 is used as a surname, tied to the place-name radical common in family names.
广 (yǎn) is close to the sound of 邝, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xìng Kuàng, shì Guǎngdōng rén.
example.english: His surname is Kuang, and he is from Guangdong.
example.fact: 邝 is a surname concentrated especially in Guangdong and among overseas Chinese communities in Southeast Asia, tracing back to a branch of the ancient Kuang clan.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 艿 names a plant, used in 芋艿 (taro).
乃 (nǎi) gives the sound — an exact match with 艿's reading.

example.pinyin: Cānzhuō shàng yǒu yì pán yùnǎi.
example.english: There is a plate of taro on the dinner table.
example.fact: 芋艿 (yùnǎi) is a regional name for taro used especially around Shanghai, where the starchy root is a popular ingredient in autumn desserts and soups.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 趺 names the instep, the top part of the foot.
夫 (fū) gives the sound — an exact match with 趺's reading.

example.pinyin: Fóxiàng chángcháng chéng fūzuò zītài.
example.english: Buddha statues often appear in a cross-legged sitting posture.
example.fact: 趺坐 (fūzuò), the cross-legged 'lotus position,' is the standard seated posture depicted in Buddhist statues and used in meditation practice across East Asia.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲟 names the sturgeon, a fish.
寻 (xún) gives the sound — an exact match with 鲟's reading.

example.hanzi: 长江里曾经生活着中华鲟。
example.pinyin: Chángjiāng lǐ céngjīng shēnghuó zhe Zhōnghuá xún.
example.english: The Chinese sturgeon used to live in the Yangtze River.
example.fact: The Chinese sturgeon (中华鲟) is a living fossil whose lineage dates back over 140 million years, but wild populations have collapsed so severely that natural spawning in the Yangtze has not been confirmed in over a decade.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剜 describes a cutting action, to gouge or scoop out with a blade.
宛 (wǎn) is close to the sound of 剜 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 医生把伤口里的碎片剜了出来。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng bǎ shāngkǒu lǐ de suìpiàn wān le chūlái.
example.english: The doctor gouged the fragments out of the wound.
example.fact: 剜 describes cutting or scooping something out with a blade, and appears in the vivid idiom 剜肉补疮 ('cutting flesh from one place to patch a sore in another'), meaning a fix that only creates a new problem.

components.note: 纟 (silk, thread) — 绉 names crepe, a crinkled woven fabric.
刍 (chú) no longer closely resembles 绉's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā chuān zhe yì tiáo zhòushā qúnzi.
example.english: She is wearing a crepe skirt.
example.fact: 绉纱 (zhòushā), 'crepe fabric,' gets its name from its characteristically crinkled, wrinkled surface texture, woven by twisting the threads more tightly than in plain silk.

etymologyHint: The sound 虖 of pottery 缶 breaking

components.note: 缶 (an earthenware jar) ties 罅 to pottery, and by extension, any vessel with a crack.
虖 (hū, an exclamation like 'ah!') does not closely resemble 罅's sound (xià); it is traditionally read here as evoking the sound pottery makes when it cracks, giving 罅 its meaning 'crack, fissure.'

example.pinyin: Qiáng shàng chūxiàn le yí dào xiàxì.
example.english: A crack appeared in the wall.
example.fact: 罅隙 (xiàxì) means a crack or gap, and is also used figuratively in Chinese for a rift or falling-out between people, much like the English phrase 'a crack in the relationship.'

meanings: square bamboo container for food or clothing

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笥 names a woven bamboo basket or hamper.
司 (sī) is close to the sound of 笥 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Shūxìn bèi fàng jìn le zhú sì lǐ.
example.english: The letter was placed inside a bamboo box.
example.fact: 笥 named a square woven bamboo container once used across ancient China to store clothing, books, and food — a common household object that has since been replaced by boxes, chests, and drawers of other materials.

meanings: the open seam of a garment which allows freedom of movement
slit on either side of robe

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 衩 names a slit or seam in a garment.
叉 (chǎ) gives the sound — an exact match with 衩's reading.

example.pinyin: Qúnzi liǎng cè kāi le chǎ.
example.english: The skirt has slits on both sides.
example.fact: 开衩 (kāichǎ), 'a slit opening,' is the standard tailoring term in Chinese for the side slit in a qipao or skirt that allows for easier movement while keeping the garment fitted.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姣 describes feminine beauty.
交 (jiāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 姣's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā zhǎng de shífēn jiāohǎo.
example.english: She is very beautiful.
example.fact: 姣好 (jiāohǎo) is a literary term for physical beauty that appears in classical Chinese poetry, though in modern speech 漂亮 or 美丽 are far more common.

components.note: 斤 (axe) — 斫 describes an action done with a blade, to chop or hack.
石 (shí) no longer closely resembles 斫's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Gōngjiàng yòng fǔ zhuó mù.
example.english: The craftsman chops the wood with an axe.
example.fact: 斫 survives mainly in the idiom 斫轮老手 ('an old hand at chopping wheel spokes'), a phrase from the ancient philosopher Zhuangzi describing a master craftsman whose skill comes only from decades of practice, not from books.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹗 names the osprey, a fish-hawk.
咢 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 鹗's reading.

example.hanzi: 一只鹗从天空俯冲而下。
example.pinyin: Yì zhī è cóng tiānkōng fǔchōng ér xià.
example.english: An osprey swooped down from the sky.
example.fact: The osprey (鹗) is one of the most widely distributed birds of prey in the world, found on every continent except Antarctica, and it feeds almost exclusively on fish.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 腎 names an internal organ, the kidney.
臤 (qiān) no longer closely resembles the sound of 腎 (shèn) — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it is traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 他的腎功能出現了問題。
example.pinyin: Tā de shèn gōngnéng chūxiàn le wèntí.
example.english: His kidney function has developed a problem.
example.fact: 腎 is the traditional, unsimplified form of 肾 — both are read shèn and mean "kidney"; you will see 腎 used in Chinese texts from Taiwan and Hong Kong, and in materials printed before the 1950s simplification reform.

etymologyHint: Two marks 乂 on an oracle bone

components.note: 爻 is formed of a crossed mark (乂) repeated twice over, echoing the broken and unbroken lines stacked to form a hexagram; the character names the individual lines used in divination in the I Ching (Yijing).

example.pinyin: Yìjīng yòng yáo lái biǎoshì guàxiàng.
example.english: The Book of Changes uses lines to represent hexagrams.
example.fact: Each hexagram in the I Ching (Yijing) is built from six horizontal lines, or 爻, that are either broken or unbroken — one of the oldest binary-style symbol systems in the world, over two thousand years old.

meanings: used in 獼猴|猕猴[mi2 hou2]

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 猕 names a kind of monkey, as in 猕猴 (macaque).
弥 (mí) gives the sound — an exact match with 猕's reading.

example.pinyin: Éméi Shān shàng yǒu hěn duō míhóu.
example.english: There are many macaques on Mount Emei.
example.fact: Mount Emei in Sichuan is home to thousands of wild Tibetan macaques (猕猴), which are famous for approaching and sometimes snatching food from tourists along the mountain paths.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晗 describes a time of day, just before dawn.
含 (hán) gives the sound — an exact match with 晗's reading.

example.hanzi: 天刚破晗，鸟儿就开始鸣叫。
example.pinyin: Tiān gāng pò hán, niǎor jiù kāishǐ míngjiào.
example.english: As soon as dawn broke, the birds began to sing.
example.fact: 晗 is rarely used outside of given names in modern Chinese — its meaning 'just before dawn' made it a popular character for parents naming children born in the early morning.

meanings: (literary) to cripple; to harm; to injure
etymologyHint: A metal 钅 weapon 杀

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 铩 as a metal weapon, an old term for a spear or lance.
杀 (shā, 'to kill') matches 铩's sound exactly and reinforces its meaning as a lethal weapon, later extending to 'to injure, to cripple.'

example.hanzi: 士兵手持长铩冲向敌阵。
example.pinyin: Shìbīng shǒuchí cháng shā chōngxiàng dízhèn.
example.english: The soldier charged at the enemy line holding a long spear.
example.fact: 铩 named an ancient Chinese spear or lance, and the idiom 铩羽而归 (shāyǔ ér guī, 'to return with clipped feathers') describes coming home defeated, comparing a beaten army to a bird whose wings have been damaged.

components.note: 穴 (cave, hole) — 窕 describes something slender and graceful, as if hollowed out and slim.
兆 (zhào) no longer closely resembles 窕's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā de shēncái yǎotiǎo dòngrén.
example.english: Her figure is slender and graceful.
example.fact: 窈窕 (yǎotiǎo) is a compliment for a graceful figure that dates back to the opening poem of the Book of Songs (Shijing), China's oldest collection of poetry, compiled over two thousand years ago.

meanings: (coll.) three (cannot be followed by a measure word)
three (colloquial equivalent of 三個|三个)

components.note: 三 (three) — 仨 is a colloquial way to say 'three,' built directly from the numeral.
三 (sān) is close to the sound of 仨, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen sā yìqǐ qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: The three of us went to see a movie together.
example.fact: 仨 is a colloquial contraction that packs the meaning of 三个 ('three of') into a single syllable, but unlike 三个, it can never be followed by a measure word or noun — you can only say 我们仨, never 仨个人.

meanings: to push over or push back

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 搡 describes an action of the hand, to shove or push.
桑 (sāng) is close to the sound of 搡 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā yìbǎ jiāng mén sǎngkāi.
example.english: He shoved the door open with one hand.
example.fact: 搡 describes a rough, forceful push, and appears in the northern Chinese colloquial phrase 推推搡搡 (tuī tuī sǎng sǎng), describing a crowd jostling and shoving against each other.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崴 describes something high and precipitous, like a mountain, and by extension to twist or sprain an ankle on uneven ground.
威 (wēi) is close to the sound of 崴, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā bù xiǎoxīn wǎi le jiǎo.
example.english: He accidentally sprained his ankle.
example.fact: 崴脚 (wǎijiǎo), 'to sprain one's ankle,' is one of the most common sports injuries worldwide, usually caused by the foot rolling outward onto uneven ground.

components.note: 酉 (wine, fermented drink) — 酢 names vinegar, a fermented product; also describes toasting one's host.
乍 (zhà) no longer closely resembles 酢's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 客人向主人回敬了一杯酢酒。
example.pinyin: Kèrén xiàng zhǔrén huíjìng le yì bēi zuò jiǔ.
example.english: The guest returned a toast to the host.
example.fact: 酢 is the character behind 应酬 (yìngchou, 'social obligations, wining and dining'), which literally traces back to the ritual of guests and hosts exchanging toasts at a banquet.

components.note: 木 (wood) reflects that a 檄 was a wooden tablet or dispatch, used in ancient China to post urgent military proclamations or calls to arms.
敫 (jiǎo) is not obviously connected to 檄's sound (xí) today; it originally suggested something radiating or spreading outward, which fits how a 檄 dispatch was meant to circulate widely and urgently.

example.hanzi: 将军发布了一篇讨伐的檄文。
example.pinyin: Jiāngjūn fābù le yì piān tǎofá de xíwén.
example.english: The general issued a proclamation calling for a punitive campaign.
example.fact: 檄文 (xíwén) named the wooden dispatch boards ancient Chinese armies used to publicly announce a call to arms — the genre survives today as a term for any strongly worded public denunciation.

etymologyHint: Kindness 仁 toward a woman 女

components.note: 亻 (person) combines with 二 above 女 to form an embedded 仁 ('kindness, benevolence') over 女 (woman); the traditional gloss reads 佞 as excessive, insincere 'kindness' aimed at someone — the source of its meaning 'flattery, glib cunning.'
女 (woman) sits at the base of the character, completing the traditional image of insincere charm.

example.pinyin: Tā wéirén jiānnìng, guànyú féngyíng.
example.english: He is cunning and flattering, always currying favor.
example.fact: 奸佞 (jiānnìng) is the standard term in Chinese historical dramas for a scheming court flatterer — a stock villain role in imperial-era politics, blamed in official histories for misleading emperors.

components.note: 孑 is traditionally explained as a variant of 子 (child) missing part of a limb, a visual image of something incomplete or cut short — the source of its meaning 'remaining, left over, all alone.'

example.pinyin: Tā jiérán yìshēn, wúyī wúkào.
example.english: He is all alone, with no one to depend on.
example.fact: 孑然一身 (jiérán yìshēn), 'utterly alone,' is a set four-character phrase built entirely around this one rare character 孑, which by itself simply means 'solitary, remaining.'

components.note: 王 (a form of 玉, jade) — 璀 ties the character to gems and their glittering luster.
崔 (cuī) is close to the sound of 璀 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 钻石在灯光下璀璨发光。
example.pinyin: Zuànshí zài dēngguāng xià cuǐcàn fāguāng.
example.english: The diamond sparkles brilliantly under the light.
example.fact: 璀 almost never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists overwhelmingly as the first half of the fixed compound 璀璨 ('brilliant, dazzling'), describing the sparkle of gems, stars, or lights.

meanings: name of a river in Sichuan

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 岷 names a mountain and a river in Sichuan.
民 (mín) gives the sound — an exact match with 岷's reading.

example.pinyin: Mínjiāng fāyuán yú Sìchuān.
example.english: The Min River originates in Sichuan.
example.fact: The Min River (岷江) was long mistaken by ancient Chinese geographers for the true source of the Yangtze, until Ming-dynasty explorer Xu Xiake proved the Jinsha River was the actual headwater in the 17th century.

components.note: 舛 depicts a pair of feet pointing in opposite directions — a picture of misstep or contrariness that gives the character its meaning 'to oppose, to err, to be at odds.'

example.hanzi: 他的命运总是十分舛错。
example.pinyin: Tā de mìngyùn zǒngshì shífēn chuǎncuò.
example.english: His fate is always full of misfortune.
example.fact: 命运多舛 (mìngyùn duōchuǎn), 'a fate full of misfortune,' is a common phrase in Chinese biographies and eulogies to describe someone whose life was marked by repeated hardship.

meanings: former or literary name for Nanning (in Guangxi)
etymologyHint: The area 邑 around a river 巛

components.note: 巛 (a flowing stream, related to 川) surrounds the character, picturing water encircling a settlement.
邑 (a city, a settlement) sits below the water; together they depict 'a city surrounded by a moat or river,' the old literal sense of 邕, later the name for the city of Nanning.

example.hanzi: 邕江是南宁的重要水道。
example.pinyin: Yōngjiāng shì Nánníng de zhòngyào shuǐdào.
example.english: The Yong River is an important waterway in Nanning.
example.fact: 邕 was the old literary name for the city of Nanning, the capital of Guangxi, and the character still appears today in the city's official abbreviation and in local place names.

components.note: 门 (door, gate) reflects 闿's meaning 'to open' — literally opening a door or gate.
岂 carries an old alternate reading 'kǎi' — the same one preserved in 凯 (kǎi, 'triumphant') — which closely matches 闿's sound; both 'open' and 'triumphant' carry a sense of release or unblocking.

example.pinyin: Chéngmén zhōngyú kǎi kāi le.
example.english: The city gate finally opened.
example.fact: 闿 is an archaic literary word for 'open, peaceful' that survives almost exclusively in given names and in classical texts, having been replaced by 开 in everyday Mandarin.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铂 names platinum, a metal.
白 (bái) is close to the sound of 铂, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhè méi jièzhi shì chún bójīn de.
example.english: This ring is made of pure platinum.
example.fact: Platinum (铂) is roughly 30 times rarer than gold in the Earth's crust, which is one reason platinum jewelry commands a premium price despite the metal's duller shine compared to gold.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霁 describes weather clearing up after rain.
齐 (qí) is close to the sound of 霁, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Yǔ hòu tiānqì jì lǎng.
example.english: The weather cleared up bright after the rain.
example.fact: 霁 gives its name to two famous Qing-dynasty porcelain glazes fired at the Jingdezhen kilns — 霁红 (sacrificial red) and 霁蓝 (sacrificial blue) — among the most prized colors in classical Chinese ceramics.

components.note: 牛 (ox) — 犒 relates to rewarding soldiers, historically with cattle and food.
高 (gāo) is close to the sound of 犒, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 将军犒劳了得胜的士兵。
example.pinyin: Jiāngjūn kàoláo le déshèng de shìbīng.
example.english: The general rewarded the victorious soldiers.
example.fact: 犒劳 (kàoláo), 'to reward with food and drink,' describes a custom recorded throughout Chinese military history, in which returning troops were feted with a feast to honor their service.

meanings: to reheat cold food by steaming it
etymologyHint: Distilled 留 wine 饣; 留 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 (food) ties 馏 to cooking and food preparation.
留 shares 馏's exact sound (liú) and means 'to remain, to stay'; combined with 饣, it evokes vapor 'staying behind' as liquid during distillation or steaming.

example.pinyin: Zhè dào cài xūyào gé shuǐ zhēngliú.
example.english: This dish needs to be steamed using a water bath.
example.fact: 蒸馏 (zhēngliú), 'to distill,' names the same basic process used to purify water, produce essential oils, and make spirits like baijiu — heating a liquid until it becomes vapor, then cooling that vapor back into a purer liquid.

etymologyHint: Separated 或 by a gate 门

components.note: 门 (gate, door) frames the character, evoking a threshold one must cross.
或 (huò, 'perhaps, or') does not closely match 阈's sound (yù); here it suggests a boundary or demarcated area, reinforcing 阈's meaning 'threshold, the dividing line between states.'

example.hanzi: 疼痛已经超过了他的忍耐阈值。
example.pinyin: Téngtòng yǐjīng chāoguò le tā de rěnnài yùzhí.
example.english: The pain has already exceeded his threshold of tolerance.
example.fact: 阈值 (yùzhí) is the standard Chinese term for 'threshold' in science and engineering, used for concepts like the minimum stimulus needed to trigger a nerve response or the trigger point for a computer alert.

components.note: 鹿 (deer) — 麋 names the elk or moose, a deer-like animal.
米 (mǐ) is close to the sound of 麋 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 东北的森林里生活着麋鹿。
example.pinyin: Dōngběi de sēnlín lǐ shēnghuó zhe mílù.
example.english: Milu deer live in the forests of the northeast.
example.fact: 麋鹿 (mílù), also called Père David's deer, went extinct in the wild in China but survived only in European parks — the species was later reintroduced to Chinese nature reserves from that captive stock in the 1980s.

components.note: 鹿 (deer) — 麒 names a mythical deer-like creature, as in 麒麟 (qílín, the Chinese unicorn).
其 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 麒's reading.

example.hanzi: 麒麟是中国神话中的吉祥神兽。
example.pinyin: Qílín shì Zhōngguó shénhuà zhōng de jíxiáng shénshòu.
example.english: The qilin is an auspicious mythical creature in Chinese mythology.
example.fact: 麒麟 (qílín) is a composite mythical creature said to appear only during times of peace and wise rulership — in 1414, a giraffe brought to the Ming court from East Africa by Admiral Zheng He's fleet was hailed by officials as a living qilin.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苁 names a medicinal herb.
从 (cóng) is close to the sound of 苁 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 肉苁蓉是一种珍贵的中药材。
example.pinyin: Ròucōngróng shì yì zhǒng zhēnguì de zhōngyào cái.
example.english: Cistanche is a precious Chinese medicinal herb.
example.fact: 肉苁蓉 (ròucōngróng), or cistanche, is a parasitic desert plant with no roots or leaves of its own — it survives entirely by tapping into the root systems of nearby desert shrubs for water and nutrients.

meanings: to press (with one's finger or hand)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摁 describes an action of the hand, to press.
恩 (ēn) is close to the sound of 摁 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā èn xià le ménlíng de ànniǔ.
example.english: He pressed the doorbell button.
example.fact: 摁 is a colloquial, largely northern Chinese verb for 'to press,' used interchangeably with the more formal 按 in everyday speech about pressing buttons, switches, or someone's shoulder.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涔 names a river and describes an overflow of water.
岑 (cén) gives the sound — an exact match with 涔's reading.

example.pinyin: Shāngǔ lǐ céncén de xià zhe yǔ.
example.english: Rain falls steadily and heavily in the valley.
example.fact: 涔涔 (céncén) describes rain falling steadily or sweat and tears streaming down continuously — a doubled form that, like many reduplicated Chinese adjectives, intensifies the sense of an ongoing, unbroken flow.

components.note: 宀 (roof, house) — 宥 relates to an act extended from a position of authority, to forgive or pardon.
有 (yǒu) is close to the sound of 宥 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 希望上级能宥恕他的过失。
example.pinyin: Xīwàng shàngjí néng yòushù tā de guòshī.
example.english: He hopes his superior can forgive his mistake.
example.fact: 宥 appears in the classical legal term 三宥 ('three pardons'), an ancient Chinese judicial principle requiring judges to consider mitigating circumstances, such as ignorance or mental illness, before sentencing.

etymologyHint: A woman 女 who appears forward or open 开

components.note: 女 (woman) ties 妍 to feminine beauty.
开 ('open') suggests a bright, open expression on a face — giving 妍 its meaning 'beautiful, becoming.'

example.pinyin: Mǔdan huā kāi de shífēn yánlì.
example.english: The peony blossoms are strikingly beautiful.
example.fact: 百花争妍 (bǎihuā zhēngyán), 'a hundred flowers vying in beauty,' is a stock phrase in Chinese garden and flower writing, and 妍 rarely appears outside of this kind of poetic description of beauty.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铤 names a metal ingot.
廷 (tíng) is close to the sound of 铤, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 银铤是古代的一种货币形式。
example.pinyin: Yín dìng shì gǔdài de yì zhǒng huòbì xíngshì.
example.english: Silver ingots were a form of currency in ancient times.
example.fact: 银铤 (yíndìng), silver ingots, were used as a standard unit of currency and taxation in imperial China for centuries, predating the widespread minting of round silver coins by hundreds of years.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锷 names the sharp edge of a metal blade.
咢 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 锷's reading.

example.pinyin: Bǎojiàn de è rèn shífēn ruìlì.
example.english: The sword's blade edge is extremely sharp.
example.fact: 锷 names specifically the sharp cutting edge of a sword blade, and appears in the poetic phrase 剑锷 used throughout classical Chinese martial and heroic literature.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗲 describes an affected, coy manner of speaking.
爹 (diē) is close to the sound of 嗲, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā shuōhuà yǒudiǎn diǎshēng diǎqì.
example.english: She talks in a rather coy, babyish way.
example.fact: 嗲声嗲气 (diǎshēng diǎqì) describes an affectedly sweet, childish way of speaking, a term especially associated with the Shanghainese-influenced Mandarin stereotype of a coquettish speaking style.

etymologyHint: To plan 忄 for a battle 军; 军 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) marks 恽 as a mental activity — thinking, planning, deliberating.
军 (jūn, 'army, military') shares little more than a final vowel sound with 恽 (yùn); its sense of organizing an army lines up loosely with 恽's meaning 'to devise, to deliberate.'

example.hanzi: 恽是一个不太常见的姓。
example.pinyin: Yùn shì yí gè bú tài chángjiàn de xìng.
example.english: Yun is a fairly uncommon surname.
example.fact: 恽 today survives almost entirely as a surname — the modern painter Yun Shouping (恽寿平), a founding figure of the Qing-dynasty 'Boneless' flower-painting style, is one of its most famous bearers.

components.note: 鹿 (deer) — 麂 names the muntjac, a small deer.
几 (jǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 麂's reading.

example.hanzi: 森林里出现了一只麂子。
example.pinyin: Sēnlín lǐ chūxiàn le yì zhī jǐzi.
example.english: A muntjac appeared in the forest.
example.fact: The muntjac (麂), sometimes called the 'barking deer,' is named for its sharp, dog-like bark used as an alarm call — one of the few deer species known for making this sound.

etymologyHint: "Wild goose" 雁 money 贝; 雁 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 雁 shares 赝's exact sound (yàn) and means 'wild goose'; one theory holds that goose down was sometimes passed off as a finer fur, which is how this element came to signal 'fake, counterfeit.'
贝 (money, valuables) ties 赝 to something of supposed worth — specifically, a forged or counterfeit item passed off as genuine.

example.pinyin: Zhè fú huà bèi jiàndìng wéi yànpǐn.
example.english: This painting was identified as a fake.
example.fact: 赝品 (yànpǐn), 'a forged or counterfeit item,' is the standard term used across the Chinese art and antiques market to describe forgeries — a serious concern given how much of the market for classical calligraphy and painting has historically involved fakes.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 胛 names a part of the body, the shoulder blade.
甲 (jiǎ) gives the sound — an exact match with 胛's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的胛骨在事故中受伤了。
example.pinyin: Tā de jiǎgǔ zài shìgù zhōng shòushāng le.
example.english: His shoulder blade was injured in the accident.
example.fact: 肩胛骨 (jiānjiǎgǔ), the shoulder blade, is a flat, triangular bone that anchors many of the muscles used to move the arm — one of the few major bones in the body that is not directly connected to another bone by a joint.

meanings: (Cant.) a final particle indicating doing something to the full extent possible

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哂 describes a mouth-related action, to smile or sneer.
西 (xī) no longer closely resembles 哂's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā shěnxiào zhe yáo le yáo tóu.
example.english: He shook his head with a mocking smile.
example.fact: 哂笑 (shěnxiào), 'to smirk, to sneer,' is a literary word almost always used to describe a condescending or mocking smile, distinct from the warmth of an ordinary 微笑 (a smile).

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 撷 describes an action of the hand, to gather or pick up.
颉 (xié) gives the sound — an exact match with 撷's reading.

example.hanzi: 她从书中撷取了一些精彩的段落。
example.pinyin: Tā cóng shū zhōng xiéqǔ le yìxiē jīngcǎi de duànluò.
example.english: She extracted some excellent passages from the book.
example.fact: 撷取 (xiéqǔ), 'to pick out and gather,' is commonly used figuratively in Chinese writing for selecting the best ideas or excerpts from a larger body of work, much like picking the finest flowers from a garden.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呶 describes a mouth-related action, to clamor or talk noisily.
奴 (nú) is close to the sound of 呶, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 孩子们呶呶不休地争吵。
example.pinyin: Háizimen náonáo bùxiū de zhēngchǎo.
example.english: The children argued on and on noisily.
example.fact: 呶呶不休 (náonáo bùxiū), 'to chatter on endlessly,' is a four-character idiom used to criticize someone who talks too much without stopping, regardless of whether anyone is listening.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噘 describes a mouth-related action, to pout.
厥 (jué) is close to the sound of 噘 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Xiǎo nǚhái juē zhe zuǐ bù gāoxìng.
example.english: The little girl pouted, unhappy.
example.fact: 噘嘴 (juēzuǐ), 'to pout,' is the standard Chinese phrase for the same universal facial expression of sulky displeasure recognized across many cultures and languages.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 懔 describes a mental or emotional state, fear or awe.
禀 (bǐng) no longer closely resembles 懔's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 大家对这场灾难感到懔然。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì zhè chǎng zāinàn gǎndào lǐnrán.
example.english: Everyone felt a chill of dread at this disaster.
example.fact: 懔 shares its phonetic component 禀 with 凛 (lǐn, 'cold, severe'), and the two characters overlap so closely in meaning — both describing a chilling fear or severity — that they are often treated as near-interchangeable in classical texts.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 栎 names a type of oak tree.
乐 (lè) is close to the sound of 栎, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shān shàng zhǎng zhe jǐ kē lìshù.
example.english: A few oak trees grow on the mountain.
example.fact: 栎 names one type of oak in Chinese, though the more common everyday word for oak trees in general is 橡树 (xiàngshù), named for the acorns (橡子) they produce.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 桎 names wooden shackles or fetters.
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 桎's reading.

example.pinyin: Qiúfàn dài zhe zhìgù bèi yā zǒu.
example.english: The prisoner was led away wearing shackles and manacles.
example.fact: 桎梏 (zhìgù) distinguishes ankle shackles (桎) from wrist manacles (梏), reflecting how ancient Chinese law codes specified different restraints for different parts of the body.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霰 names a form of precipitation, sleet or graupel.
散 (sǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 霰's reading.

example.pinyin: Chuāngwài xiàqǐ le sǎn.
example.english: Sleet began falling outside the window.
example.fact: 霰 names graupel, small pellets of snow coated in a thin layer of ice that form when supercooled water droplets freeze onto a falling snowflake — meteorologists distinguish it clearly from both ordinary snow and hail.

components.note: 食 (food) — 飨 describes hosting a banquet, offering food and drink.
乡 (xiāng) is close to the sound of 飨 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Guówáng shèyàn xiǎng zhòng bīnkè.
example.english: The king held a banquet to feast all his guests.
example.fact: 飨 appears in the term 犒飨 (kàoxiǎng), an ancient ritual of feasting and rewarding troops or allies, and the character is also used metaphorically today in 以此飨读者 ('offered here to treat the reader'), a formal way authors describe presenting their work to an audience.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揄 describes an action of the hand, to lift or raise.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 揄's reading.

example.hanzi: 他忍不住揄扬自己的功劳。
example.pinyin: Tā rěnbuzhù yúyáng zìjǐ de gōngláo.
example.english: He couldn't help but boast about his own achievements.
example.fact: 揄扬 (yúyáng) means 'to praise, to extol,' and is a formal literary term historians used to describe how court officials publicized an emperor's or general's accomplishments.

meanings: (Cant.) for (a recipient of pity or sympathy)

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噔 is used to write the onomatopoeia of a thud or thump.
登 (dēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 噔's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā dēngdēng de pǎo xià le lóutī.
example.english: He ran down the stairs with thudding footsteps.
example.fact: 噔噔 (dēngdēng) is an onomatopoeia written specifically with the mouth radical 口, part of a large family of Chinese sound-effect characters used to capture footsteps, knocks, and other everyday noises in writing.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 娣 names a female family relation, a younger sister-in-law.
弟 (dì) gives the sound — an exact match with 娣's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā de dìmèi zhù zài gébì.
example.english: Her younger sister-in-law lives next door.
example.fact: 娣 named specifically the wife of one's husband's younger brother in the traditional Chinese kinship system, which once had distinct terms for in-laws that modern Mandarin has mostly collapsed into broader words like 弟媳.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 薏 names a plant, as in 薏苡 (Job's tears).
意 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 薏's reading.

example.hanzi: 薏米粥是夏天常喝的汤品。
example.pinyin: Yìmǐ zhōu shì xiàtiān cháng hē de tāngpǐn.
example.english: Job's tears porridge is a soup commonly drunk in summer.
example.fact: 薏米 (yìmǐ), Job's tears, is a grain widely used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine, believed to help clear dampness from the body, and is a common ingredient in cooling summer congee.

components.note: ⺗ (a form of 心, heart) — 忝 describes an emotional state, shame.
天 (tiān) is close to the sound of 忝 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他自觉才疏学浅，深感忝愧。
example.pinyin: Tā zìjué cáishū xuéqiǎn, shēngǎn tiǎnkuì.
example.english: He felt his talent and learning were shallow, and was deeply ashamed.
example.fact: 忝 appears in the humble, self-deprecating phrase 忝列门墙 ('to be unworthily counted among the disciples'), a set expression once used by students to modestly describe studying under a respected teacher.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咤 describes a mouth-related action, to shout or bellow.
宅 (zhái) is close to the sound of 咤, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā fènnù de chìzhà nùhǒu.
example.english: He roared angrily in a furious shout.
example.fact: 叱咤风云 (chìzhà fēngyún), 'to command the winds and clouds with a shout,' is a vivid four-character idiom describing someone whose power and influence seem to dominate everything around them.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗵 is used to write the onomatopoeia of a thud or thump.
通 (tōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 嗵's reading.

example.hanzi: 石头嗵地一声掉进了水里。
example.pinyin: Shítou tōng de yì shēng diào jìn le shuǐ lǐ.
example.english: The stone fell into the water with a plop.
example.fact: 嗵 is a purely onomatopoeic character with no meaning beyond the thud or splash sound it represents, existing solely to let writers capture a specific noise in text.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, to move) — 迤 describes a winding, indirect path.
也 (yě) is close to the sound of 迤, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shānlù yǐlǐ xiàng yuǎnchù yánshēn.
example.english: The mountain path winds and stretches off into the distance.
example.fact: 逶迤 (wēiyí) describes a road, river, or mountain range that winds gently into the distance, and is a favorite word in Chinese travel writing and poetry for describing scenic, meandering landscapes.

components.note: 卉 (flowers, plants) suggests a decorative, floral pattern.

贝 (a shell, an object of value) combines with 卉 to evoke something richly adorned; that sense of grand ornamentation extended to 贲's meaning 'vigorous, forging ahead,' as in 虎贲 (hǔbēn, 'valiant warrior').

example.hanzi: 虎贲是古代皇帝的精锐卫队。
example.pinyin: Hǔbēn shì gǔdài huángdì de jīngruì wèiduì.
example.english: The Tiger Guard was the ancient emperor's elite bodyguard.
example.fact: 虎贲 (hǔbēn), 'valiant as a tiger,' was the name of an elite imperial guard unit recorded as far back as the Zhou dynasty, tasked specifically with protecting the ruler's person.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 胪 names the belly, and by extension to display or arrange in order.
卢 (lú) gives the sound — an exact match with 胪's reading.

example.hanzi: 典礼上依次胪列了嘉宾名单。
example.pinyin: Diǎnlǐ shàng yīcì lúliè le jiābīn míngdān.
example.english: The list of honored guests was read out in order at the ceremony.
example.fact: 胪列 (lúliè), 'to list out in order,' is a formal, literary term still occasionally used in official Chinese documents and ceremonies for enumerating items one after another.

components.note: 金 (metal) — 鍪 names an object made of metal, an iron pot or helmet.
敄 (wù) no longer closely resembles the sound of 鍪 (móu) — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it is traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 考古学家发掘出一件青铜鍪。
example.pinyin: Kǎogǔ xuéjiā fājué chū yí jiàn qīngtóng móu.
example.english: Archaeologists unearthed a bronze cooking pot.
example.fact: 鍪 named an ancient cooking vessel and, in a related sense, a soldier's metal helmet — Chinese archaeologists have recovered bronze examples of both from tombs dating back over two thousand years.

meanings: old name of a river in Jiangxi

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泸 names a river.
卢 (lú) gives the sound — an exact match with 泸's reading.

example.hanzi: 泸州是中国著名的酒乡。
example.pinyin: Lúzhōu shì Zhōngguó zhùmíng de jiǔxiāng.
example.english: Luzhou is a famous wine-producing region in China.
example.fact: Luzhou (泸州), in Sichuan, is one of China's most celebrated centers for producing baijiu, the strong distilled liquor, and is home to a distillery with continuously operating fermentation pits dating back centuries.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 蔫 describes a plant wilting or withering.
焉 (yān) no longer closely resembles 蔫's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Huāpíng lǐ de huā yǐjīng niān le.
example.english: The flowers in the vase have already wilted.
example.fact: 蔫 describes a plant losing its firmness and drooping from lack of water, and is also used colloquially in Chinese to describe a person who seems listless or low-spirited, as in 蔫头蔫脑.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 刈 describes a cutting action, to reap or mow.
乂 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 刈's reading.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín zhèngzài yìgē dàozi.
example.english: The farmers are reaping the rice.
example.fact: 刈 is one of the oldest Chinese characters for cutting or reaping grain, attested in ancient bronze inscriptions describing harvesting crops with a sickle thousands of years ago.

etymologyHint: Someone 亻 in love 喜; 喜 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) marks 僖 as a description of a person's mood or manner.
喜 (xǐ, 'happy, joyful') is close to the sound of 僖 (xī) — the same syllable, different tone — and lends 僖 its meaning 'joy, gladness.'

example.hanzi: 鲁僖公是春秋时期的君主。
example.pinyin: Lǔ Xī Gōng shì Chūnqiū shíqī de jūnzhǔ.
example.english: Duke Xi of Lu was a ruler during the Spring and Autumn period.
example.fact: 僖 appears almost exclusively in the posthumous titles of ancient Chinese rulers, such as Duke Xi of Lu (鲁僖公), a state ruler whose reign is recorded in the classic historical text Zuo Zhuan.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咿 is used to write a small vocal sound, a creak or laugh.
伊 (yī) gives the sound — an exact match with 咿's reading.

example.pinyin: Ménzhóu fāchū yīyā de shēngyīn.
example.english: The door hinge made a creaking sound.
example.fact: 咿呀 (yīyā) is an onomatopoeia for a creaking hinge or a baby's babbling, and the same two syllables also appear in 咿呀学语 (yīyā xuéyǔ), a phrase describing a toddler just beginning to learn to speak.

meanings: used in 鵪鶉|鹌鹑[an1 chun2]

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹌 names the quail, a bird.
奄 (yǎn) is close to the sound of 鹌, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 餐厅里有一道鹌鹑蛋料理。
example.pinyin: Cāntīng lǐ yǒu yí dào ānchún dàn liàolǐ.
example.english: The restaurant has a quail egg dish.
example.fact: 鹌鹑 (ānchún), the quail, lays eggs that are only about a fifth the size of a chicken egg, yet proportionally richer in several vitamins and minerals, which is why quail eggs are prized as a delicacy in Chinese cooking.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗪 is a mouth-radical marker used to build characters for chemical transliterations, like piperazine.
秦 (qín) gives the sound — an exact match with 嗪's reading.

example.hanzi: 哌嗪是一种常见的化学药品。
example.pinyin: Pàiqín shì yì zhǒng chángjiàn de huàxué yàopǐn.
example.english: Piperazine is a common chemical medicine.
example.fact: 嗪 belongs to a set of characters invented in the twentieth century purely to transliterate Western chemical names into Chinese, with the mouth radical 口 marking that the character exists mainly for its sound, not an inherited meaning.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 茏 names tall grass or water-weeds.
龙 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 茏's reading.

example.hanzi: 池塘边长满了葱茏的水草。
example.pinyin: Chítáng biān zhǎng mǎn le cōnglóng de shuǐcǎo.
example.english: Lush water-weeds grow thickly along the edge of the pond.
example.fact: 葱茏 (cōnglóng) describes vegetation that is lush, dense, and vividly green, a word favored in Chinese nature writing to evoke the height of summer growth.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 茯 names a medicinal fungus, as in 茯苓.
伏 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 茯's reading.

example.hanzi: 茯苓是一种常用的中药。
example.pinyin: Fúlíng shì yì zhǒng chángyòng de zhōngyào.
example.english: Poria is a commonly used ingredient in Chinese medicine.
example.fact: 茯苓 (fúlíng), poria, is actually a fungus that grows on the roots of pine trees, not a plant, despite being written with the grass radical 艹 like most herbs in Chinese materia medica.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 岫 names a mountain peak or cave.
由 (yóu) no longer closely resembles 岫's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Yúnwù liáorào zài shānxiù zhījiān.
example.english: Clouds and mist swirl among the mountain peaks.
example.fact: 岫 is a literary word for a mountain peak or cave that appears often in classical Chinese landscape poetry, evoking misty, secluded scenery rather than describing an ordinary hill.

meanings: used in 崢嶸|峥嵘[zheng1 rong2]

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 嵘 describes something towering, like a steep mountain peak.
荣 (róng) gives the sound — an exact match with 嵘's reading.

example.pinyin: Shānfēng zhēngróng, qìshì xióngwěi.
example.english: The mountain peaks rise sharply, with a majestic bearing.
example.fact: 峥嵘 (zhēngróng) describes towering, jagged peaks, and is also used figuratively in the phrase 峥嵘岁月 ("turbulent, momentous years") to describe an extraordinary period in someone's life or in history.

meanings: used in 軲轆|轱辘[gu1 lu5]

components.note: 车 (cart, vehicle) — 轱 names a wheel and describes turning or revolving.
古 (gǔ) is close to the sound of 轱 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 自行车的轱辘转得很快。
example.pinyin: Zìxíngchē de gūlu zhuàn de hěn kuài.
example.english: The bicycle's wheel spins very fast.
example.fact: 轱辘 (gūlu) is a colloquial northern Chinese word for 'wheel,' more common in everyday spoken Mandarin around Beijing than the formal word 轮子, and it can also be used as a verb meaning 'to roll.'

components.note: 心 (heart, mind) — 怼 describes an emotional state, resentment or hatred.
对 (duì) gives the sound — an exact match with 怼's reading.

example.hanzi: 他心里一直怼着这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā xīnlǐ yìzhí duì zhe zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He has been resentful about this matter all along.
example.fact: 怼 was a fairly obscure classical character for resentment until around 2016, when it suddenly became popular internet slang in the sense 'to argue with, to call out,' as in 互怼 ('to trade insults with each other').

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铨 originally referred to a metal scale or balance used for weighing, extended to 'to weigh, to select.'
全 (quán) gives the sound — an exact match with 铨's reading.

example.hanzi: 考试成绩由专门机构铨选。
example.pinyin: Kǎoshì chéngjì yóu zhuānmén jīgòu quánxuǎn.
example.english: Exam results are reviewed and selected by a specialized agency.
example.fact: 铨选 (quánxuǎn) was the formal historical term for the imperial process of examining and appointing officials to government posts, a core part of China's centuries-old civil service examination system.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 昕 describes a time of day, dawn or early morning.
斤 (jīn) is close to the sound of 昕, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xíguàn zài xīndàn shí qǐchuáng.
example.english: He is used to getting up at first light.
example.fact: 昕 is a literary word for the very first light of dawn, and today it survives mainly as a popular character in given names, chosen by parents for its bright, hopeful meaning.

components.note: 阝 (place, settlement) — 郢 was an ancient place name, the capital of the state of Chu.
呈 (chéng) no longer closely resembles 郢's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Yǐngdū céng shì Chǔguó de dūchéng.
example.english: Ying was once the capital city of the state of Chu.
example.fact: 郢 (Yǐng) was the capital of the ancient state of Chu for centuries during the Warring States period, near modern-day Jingzhou in Hubei, and appears often in classical Chinese poetry and history.

etymologyHint: The sound a sheep 羊 makes with its mouth 口

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks 咩 as a sound made vocally.
羊 (sheep, goat) identifies the animal; together they spell out 咩, the onomatopoeia for a sheep's bleat, much like English 'baa.'

example.pinyin: Xiǎoyáng miēmiē de jiào zhe.
example.english: The little lamb bleats 'baa, baa.'
example.fact: 咩 is a purely onomatopoeic character built to represent a sheep's cry, and the same syllable independently became a common colloquial question particle in Cantonese, unrelated to the sound of any sheep.

etymologyHint: Old 叟 food 饣; 叟 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 饣 (food) ties 馊 to something edible that has gone bad.
叟 (sǒu, 'old man') is close to the sound of 馊 (sōu) — the same syllable, different tone — and its sense of 'old, aged' extends naturally to food that has aged too long and spoiled.

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē shèngcài yǐjīng sōu le.
example.english: These leftovers have already gone rancid.
