example.fact: 馊 specifically describes food, especially cooked rice or leftovers, that has spoiled and turned sour from being left out too long — a narrower meaning than the general word 坏 ('bad, spoiled').

meanings: to make the head bald (as corporal punishment)

components.note: 髟 (hair, related to shaving) — 髡 describes a punishment involving hair, to shave the head bald.
兀 (wù) no longer closely resembles 髡's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 古代髡刑是剃去犯人的头发。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài kūnxíng shì tìqù fànrén de tóufa.
example.english: The ancient punishment of kun involved shaving off a prisoner's hair.
example.fact: 髡刑 (kūnxíng), forcibly shaving a person's head, was recorded as a formal punishment in ancient China, considered a serious humiliation at a time when long hair was deeply tied to personal dignity and Confucian values.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 澧 names a river in Hunan province.
豊 (lǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 澧's reading.

example.pinyin: Lǐshuǐ liúrù Dòngtíng Hú.
example.english: The Li River flows into Dongting Lake.
example.fact: The Li River (澧水) is one of the four major rivers feeding Dongting Lake in Hunan, one of the largest freshwater lakes in China and a crucial habitat for migratory birds.

meanings: used in 萵苣|莴苣[wo1 ju4]
used in 苣蕒菜|苣荬菜[qu3 mai5 cai4]

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苣 names a type of lettuce.
巨 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match with 苣's reading.

example.pinyin: Māma mǎi le yìxiē wōjù.
example.english: Mom bought some lettuce.
example.fact: 莴苣 (wōjù) is the general Chinese word for lettuce, and its stem variety, celtuce (莴笋), is popular in Chinese cooking specifically for its crunchy stalk, unlike Western lettuce which is grown mainly for its leaves.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 濯 describes washing something in water.
隹 (zhuī) is close to the sound of 濯, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 她把衣服放进水里濯洗。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yīfu fàng jìn shuǐ lǐ zhuóxǐ.
example.english: She put the clothes in water to wash them.
example.fact: 濯 appears in the classical phrase 沧浪之水清兮，可以濯缨 ('the Canglang waters are clear, fit to wash one's cap-strings'), a line from the ancient Songs of Chu (Chu Ci) still quoted today to symbolize staying morally clean.

etymologyHint: Washing 水 one's hands 彐 in a basin 皿

components.note: 水 (water) is shown pouring down over a pair of hands at the top of the character.
皿 (a basin, a vessel) sits at the bottom, catching the water; together the character pictures someone washing their hands over a basin, the source of 盥's meaning 'to wash, especially the hands.'

example.hanzi: 他每天早上盥洗后再吃早饭。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang guànxǐ hòu zài chī zǎofàn.
example.english: He washes up every morning before eating breakfast.
example.fact: 盥洗 (guànxǐ), 'to wash up,' still gives its name to 盥洗室 (guànxǐshì), the formal Chinese term for a washroom or restroom seen on signs in hotels, offices, and airports.

etymologyHint: A girl 女 in a crib 囗

components.note: 囗 (an enclosure) pictures a crib, cradle, or protected space.
女 (girl, woman) sits inside the enclosure; together they picture a little girl kept safe in a crib, giving 囡 its meaning 'child, daughter,' chiefly in Shanghainese and other Wu dialects.

example.pinyin: Línjū jiā de nānnān cái sān suì.
example.english: The neighbor's little girl is only three years old.
example.fact: 囡囡 (nānnān) is an affectionate term for a small child used especially in Shanghai and the broader Wu-dialect region of the Yangtze Delta, rarely heard in standard Mandarin outside that area.

etymologyHint: A stone 石 used to hone 厉 blades; 厉 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 石 (stone) identifies 砺 as a type of stone — specifically, a whetstone.
厉 shares 砺's exact sound (lì) and means 'severe, sharp'; combined with 石, it names the whetstone used to hone blades to a keen edge.

example.hanzi: 他用磨刀石砺利了刀刃。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng mó dāo shí lì le dāorèn.
example.english: He sharpened the blade's edge with a whetstone.
example.fact: 砺 appears in the idiom 磨砺以须 ('to sharpen oneself in readiness'), meaning to prepare and hone one's skills in advance while waiting for the right opportunity.

components.note: 人 (person) — 佘 is used as a surname.
示 (shì) is close to the sound of 佘, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 佘太君是京剧中的著名角色。
example.pinyin: Shé Tàijūn shì jīngjù zhōng de zhùmíng juésè.
example.english: Grand Dame She is a famous character in Peking opera.
example.fact: 佘 exists in modern Chinese almost entirely as a surname, most famously carried by the legendary matriarch She Taijun (佘太君) of the Yang family generals, a folk-hero figure celebrated in Chinese opera and historical fiction.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 谶 names a prophecy or omen delivered in words.
韱 (xiān) no longer closely resembles 谶's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 这句话被认为是不祥的谶语。
example.pinyin: Zhè jù huà bèi rènwéi shì bùxiáng de chènyǔ.
example.english: This saying was considered an ominous prophecy.
example.fact: 谶语 (chènyǔ), a prophetic or omen-laden saying, played a real role in Chinese political history — rebels and dynasty founders often circulated such prophecies to claim that heaven itself endorsed their rise to power.

components.note: 杀 (to kill) — 弑 describes a specific kind of killing, murdering a ruler or parent.
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 弑's reading.

example.hanzi: 历史上曾发生过弑君的事件。
example.pinyin: Lìshǐ shàng céng fāshēng guò shì jūn de shìjiàn.
example.english: Regicide has occurred at points in history.
example.fact: 弑 is a specific legal and moral term in classical Chinese reserved only for killing a ruler or a parent — using this character rather than the ordinary word 杀 ('to kill') signaled a uniquely grave betrayal of the natural social order.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 楂 names a raft, and describes felling trees.
查 (zhā) gives the sound — an exact match with 楂's reading.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢吃山楂做的糖葫芦。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan chī shānzhā zuò de tánghúlu.
example.english: He likes to eat candied hawthorn skewers.
example.fact: 山楂 (shānzhā), hawthorn berries, are the key ingredient in 冰糖葫芦, a classic Beijing street snack of fruit skewers dipped in hardened sugar syrup, prized for the berries' natural tartness.

components.note: 羽 (feather) — 翦 names a cutting tool, scissors, related to trimming feathers or cloth.
前 (qián) is close to the sound of 翦, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 将军下令翦除叛军的势力。
example.pinyin: Jiāngjūn xiàlìng jiǎnchú pànjūn de shìlì.
example.english: The general ordered the rebel forces to be wiped out.
example.fact: 翦 is a variant of 剪 ('to cut, scissors') that also carries the extended meaning 'to eliminate, to annihilate,' as in the historical phrase 翦灭六国 describing the Qin state's conquest of its six rival states.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 怩 describes an emotional state, shyness or embarrassment.
尼 (ní) gives the sound — an exact match with 怩's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā niǔní de bù gǎn kāikǒu.
example.english: He was too shy and embarrassed to speak up.
example.fact: 忸怩 (niǔní) describes a bashful, self-conscious hesitation, and almost always appears in the fixed phrase 忸怩不安 ('fidgeting with embarrassment'), rather than being split apart into separate words.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蠼 names an insect, as in 蠼螋 (an earwig).
矍 (jué) no longer closely resembles 蠼's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 花园里发现了一只蠼螋。
example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ fāxiàn le yì zhī qúsōu.
example.english: An earwig was found in the garden.
example.fact: 蠼螋 (qúsōu), the earwig, is named for the pincer-like appendages at the tip of its abdomen, though contrary to the old folk myth its name inspired in English, it does not actually burrow into human ears.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霏 describes falling snow or rain.
非 (fēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 霏's reading.

example.pinyin: Chuāng wài yǔxuě fēifēi.
example.english: Outside the window, rain and snow are falling steadily.
example.fact: 雨雪霏霏 (yǔxuě fēifēi), 'rain and snow falling thick and fast,' is a line straight from the Book of Songs (Shijing), China's oldest poetry collection, still quoted today to evoke a heavy snowfall.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 楹 names a wooden pillar or column.
盈 (yíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 楹's reading.

example.pinyin: Dàdiàn qián lì zhe liǎng gēn yíngzhù.
example.english: Two pillars stand in front of the main hall.
example.fact: 楹联 (yínglián), the paired scrolls of poetic couplets hung on either side of a doorway at Lunar New Year, take their name from 楹, the pillars they were traditionally mounted on.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 讴 describes an act of speech, to sing.
区 (ōu) gives the sound — an exact match with 讴's reading.

example.hanzi: 渔民唱起了悠扬的渔家讴歌。
example.pinyin: Yúmín chàng qǐ le yōuyáng de yújiā ōugē.
example.english: The fishermen sang out a melodious fishing song.
example.fact: 讴歌 (ōugē) means both 'to sing' and, by extension, 'to sing the praises of, to extol' — a shift from a literal singing voice to a figurative expression of admiration common across many languages.

etymologyHint: Something engraved 契 in metal 钅; 契 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks 锲 as an action or tool involving metal — to carve or engrave, or a sickle-like blade.
契 (qì, 'to engrave, a contract') is close to the sound of 锲 (qiè) without being an exact match; its meaning of carving or engraving lines up directly with 锲's sense 'to cut, to engrave.'

example.hanzi: 他锲而不舍地追求自己的梦想。
example.pinyin: Tā qiè ér bù shě de zhuīqiú zìjǐ de mèngxiǎng.
example.english: He pursued his dream with unrelenting persistence.
example.fact: 锲而不舍 (qiè ér bù shě), 'to carve without letting go,' comes from the ancient philosopher Xunzi's writings and remains one of the most common Chinese idioms for describing persistence and determination today.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 慵 describes a state of mind, laziness or lethargy.
庸 (yōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 慵's reading.

example.hanzi: 假期里他变得慵懒起来。
example.pinyin: Jiàqī lǐ tā biàn de yōnglǎn qǐlái.
example.english: During the holidays he became lazy and languid.
example.fact: 慵懒 (yōnglǎn) describes a pleasant, unhurried laziness rather than pure idleness, and has become a popular lifestyle-marketing term in China for relaxed 'slow living' aesthetics, home decor, and loungewear.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 胝 names a callus on the skin.
氐 (dī) is close to the sound of 胝, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他手上长了厚厚的胼胝。
example.pinyin: Tā shǒu shàng zhǎng le hòuhòu de piánzhī.
example.english: Thick calluses have formed on his hands.
example.fact: 胼胝 (piánzhī), calluses, form when skin repeatedly rubbed or pressed thickens for protection — the same basic biological response seen in the hardened palms of manual laborers and the paws of working animals alike.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 砭 names an ancient stone needle used in acupuncture.
乏 (fá) no longer closely resembles 砭's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 古人用砭石为病人治病。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén yòng biānshí wèi bìngrén zhìbìng.
example.english: Ancient people used stone needles to treat patients.
example.fact: 砭石 (biānshí), sharpened stone needles, are considered the earliest tool of acupuncture in China, predating metal needles by thousands of years and dating back to the Stone Age.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 潍 names a river in Shandong province.
维 (wéi) gives the sound — an exact match with 潍's reading.

example.pinyin: Wéihé liújīng Shāndōng bàndǎo.
example.english: The Wei River flows through the Shandong Peninsula.
example.fact: 潍 gives its name to the city of Weifang (潍坊) in Shandong, famous across China as the historic center of kite-making and home to an annual international kite festival.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 杵 names a wooden or stone pestle.
午 (wǔ) is close to the sound of 杵, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Nǎinai yòng chǔ hé jiù dǎo mǐ.
example.english: Grandma pounds rice with a pestle and mortar.
example.fact: 杵臼 (chǔjiù), 'pestle and mortar,' is one of humanity's oldest food-processing tools, and the Chinese idiom 舂杵 recalls how grain was hulled by hand for thousands of years before mechanical mills became common.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 樾 names the shade cast by a tree.
越 (yuè) gives the sound — an exact match with 樾's reading.

example.pinyin: Lǎorén zuò zài shùyuè xià chéngliáng.
example.english: The old man sits in the shade of the trees to cool off.
example.fact: 樾 is an elegant literary word for the cool shade cast specifically by trees, a more poetic alternative to the everyday, more general word 阴凉 for shade.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 帼 names a cloth cap worn by women.
国 (guó) gives the sound — an exact match with 帼's reading.

example.hanzi: 花木兰是巾帼英雄的代表。
example.pinyin: Huā Mùlán shì jīnguó yīngxióng de dàibiǎo.
example.english: Hua Mulan is a representative heroine among women.
example.fact: 巾帼英雄 (jīnguó yīngxióng), 'heroine,' takes its name from 帼, an ornamental headdress worn by women in ancient China — the legendary warrior Hua Mulan is the most famous figure honored with this title.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 碣 names a stone tablet.
曷 (hé) no longer closely resembles 碣's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 山顶立着一块古老的碣石。
example.pinyin: Shāndǐng lì zhe yí kuài gǔlǎo de jiéshí.
example.english: An ancient stone tablet stands on the mountaintop.
example.fact: 碣石 (jiéshí) refers to an upright stone monument, often inscribed with text — the historical Jieshi Mountain on China's northern coast was visited and commemorated by the First Emperor of Qin during his tours of the empire.

components.note: 讠 (speech, words) — 诌 describes an act of speech, to make up a story or talk nonsense.
刍 (chú) no longer closely resembles 诌's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 别听他胡诌，那不是真的。
example.pinyin: Bié tīng tā húzhōu, nà bú shì zhēnde.
example.english: Don't listen to him making things up, that's not true.
example.fact: 胡诌 (húzhōu), 'to talk nonsense, to make up a story,' is a common colloquial phrase in spoken Mandarin used to dismiss something as an implausible fabrication.

meanings: used in 招徠|招徕[zhao1 lai2]

components.note: 彳 (to step, to walk) — 徕 describes movement, encouraging someone to come.
来 (lái) gives the sound — an exact match with 徕's reading.

example.hanzi: 商家推出优惠活动招徕顾客。
example.pinyin: Shāngjiā tuīchū yōuhuì huódòng zhāolái gùkè.
example.english: The store launched a promotion to attract customers.
example.fact: 招徕 (zhāolái), 'to attract customers,' is standard business vocabulary in Chinese, and 徕 itself survives today almost only in this one compound describing the act of drawing people in.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 胴 names a part of the body, the torso or large intestine.
同 (tóng) is close to the sound of 胴, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 运动员的胴体十分健美。
example.pinyin: Yùndòngyuán de dòngtǐ shífēn jiànměi.
example.english: The athlete's physique is very fit and well-built.
example.fact: 胴体 (dòngtǐ) refers to the human torso, and in butchery and food industry usage it also names a dressed animal carcass with the head and limbs removed — one character covering both a body part and a cut of meat.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钴 names cobalt, a metallic element.
古 (gǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 钴's reading.

example.pinyin: Diànchí lǐ hányǒu gǔ yuánsù.
example.english: The battery contains the element cobalt.
example.fact: Cobalt (钴) is a key ingredient in the cathodes of many lithium-ion batteries, which is why global demand for the metal surged sharply alongside the rise of smartphones and electric vehicles.

meanings: a cassock or robe of a monk

components.note: 衣 (clothing) — 裟 names a monk's robe, as in 袈裟.
沙 (shā) gives the sound — an exact match with 裟's reading.

example.pinyin: Héshang pī zhe yí jiàn jiāshā.
example.english: The monk wears a kasaya robe over his shoulders.
example.fact: 袈裟 (jiāshā) is a loanword from the ancient Indian language Sanskrit (kasaya), borrowed into Chinese along with Buddhism itself as the religion spread eastward along the Silk Road.

meanings: phonetic used in pyridine and pyrimidine

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 啶 is a mouth-radical marker used to build characters for chemical names, like pyridine.
定 (dìng) gives the sound — an exact match with 啶's reading.

example.hanzi: 吡啶是一种常见的化学溶剂。
example.pinyin: Bǐdìng shì yì zhǒng chángjiàn de huàxué róngjì.
example.english: Pyridine is a common chemical solvent.
example.fact: 啶 is a purely modern, functional character created to transliterate Western chemical suffixes like '-idine,' and by itself carries no meaning outside of naming compounds such as pyridine and pyrimidine.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铣 describes an action performed on metal, to mill.
先 (xiān) is close to the sound of 铣, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Gōngchǎng yòng jīchuáng xǐxiāo língjiàn.
example.english: The factory mills parts using a machine tool.
example.fact: 铣床 (xǐchuáng), the milling machine, is a foundational tool of modern manufacturing, using a rotating cutting tool to shave metal into precise shapes — a process this character names directly.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铱 names iridium, a metallic element.
衣 (yī) gives the sound — an exact match with 铱's reading.

example.hanzi: 铱是一种非常耐腐蚀的金属。
example.pinyin: Yī shì yì zhǒng fēicháng nài fǔshí de jīnshǔ.
example.english: Iridium is a metal that is extremely resistant to corrosion.
example.fact: Iridium (铱) is one of the densest naturally occurring elements and so chemically resistant that a platinum-iridium alloy was chosen to make the international prototype kilogram, the physical object that once defined the kilogram worldwide.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 楫 names a wooden oar.
咠 (qì) is close to the sound of 楫, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Chuánfū yònglì huádòng chuánjí.
example.english: The boatman rows the oar with force.
example.fact: 舟楫 (zhōují), 'boats and oars,' is a classical pairing used since ancient times as a byword for river and sea travel in general, appearing throughout early Chinese philosophical and historical texts.

components.note: 赤 (red) — 赭 names a reddish-brown color, ochre.
者 (zhě) gives the sound — an exact match with 赭's reading.

example.hanzi: 画家用赭石调出了土黄色。
example.pinyin: Huàjiā yòng zhěshí tiáo chū le tǔhuángsè.
example.english: The painter mixed ochre stone to get an earthy yellow color.
example.fact: 赭石 (zhěshí), ochre, is one of the oldest pigments used by humans, found in cave paintings tens of thousands of years old on multiple continents, long before any synthetic dye existed.

meanings: (bound form) moraine; rocks in shallow water

components.note: 石 (stone) — 碛 names sand and gravel, or rocks in shallow water.
责 (zé) no longer closely resembles 碛's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Shāmò zhōng yǒu yí piàn shāqì.
example.english: There is a stretch of gravelly sand in the desert.
example.fact: 碛 specifically names an expanse of sand and gravel, such as those found in the Gobi Desert, and the term 大碛 (great gravel flats) appears repeatedly in classical Chinese accounts of Silk Road travel.

components.note: 酉 (wine, a fermented or distilled liquid) — 酊 relates to being drunk, and to a liquid tincture.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 酊's reading.

example.hanzi: 医生用碘酊为伤口消毒。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng yòng diǎndīng wèi shāngkǒu xiāodú.
example.english: The doctor disinfects the wound with iodine tincture.
example.fact: 碘酊 (diǎndīng), iodine tincture, is a classic antiseptic once found in nearly every household first-aid kit in China, though modern medicine now more often recommends milder disinfectants for everyday cuts.

meanings: a mountain demon resembling a tiger

components.note: 鬼 (ghost, demon) — 魑 names a mountain demon.
离 (chī) gives the sound — an exact match with 魑's reading.

example.hanzi: 传说中魑魅藏在深山里。
example.pinyin: Chuánshuō zhōng chīmèi cáng zài shēnshān lǐ.
example.english: Legend has it that mountain demons hide deep in the mountains.
example.fact: 魑魅魍魉 (chīmèi wǎngliǎng), naming four distinct kinds of mountain and river demons, is a classical four-character idiom still used today to mean 'all sorts of evil people' rather than literal monsters.

components.note: 酉 (wine, here extended to chemical compounds) — 醛 names an aldehyde, a class of organic chemical.
荃 (quán) gives the sound — an exact match with 醛's reading.

example.hanzi: 甲醛是一种有害的化学物质。
example.pinyin: Jiǎquán shì yì zhǒng yǒuhài de huàxué wùzhì.
example.english: Formaldehyde is a harmful chemical substance.
example.fact: 甲醛 (jiǎquán), formaldehyde, is naturally released by new furniture and building materials over time, which is why newly renovated homes and offices in China are commonly aired out for weeks before people move in.

meanings: cut off the flesh as punishment

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剐 describes a cutting action, to cut flesh from bone.
呙 (guō) is close to the sound of 剐, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古代有一种剐刑的酷刑。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài yǒu yì zhǒng guǎxíng de kùxíng.
example.english: In ancient times there was a brutal punishment of dismemberment.
example.fact: 剐 names a form of execution recorded in imperial Chinese legal history that involved cutting the flesh from the body piece by piece — one of several punishments abolished during the legal reforms of the late Qing dynasty.

components.note: 田 (field) — 畦 names a plot or section of farmland.
圭 (guī) no longer closely resembles 畦's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 农民在菜畦里种上了白菜。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín zài càiqí lǐ zhòng shàng le báicài.
example.english: The farmer planted cabbage in the vegetable plot.
example.fact: 菜畦 (càiqí) names the small, raised rectangular plots used to organize a vegetable garden, a layout still commonly seen in Chinese farms and home gardens today for keeping different crops separated.

components.note: 阝 (a mound, hill, related to 阜) — 陂 names an embankment or a pool held back by one.
皮 (pí) no longer closely resembles 陂's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 村外有一个古老的陂塘。
example.pinyin: Cūn wài yǒu yí gè gǔlǎo de bēitáng.
example.english: There is an ancient reservoir pond outside the village.
example.fact: 陂塘 (bēitáng), small dammed ponds for irrigation, are part of a water-management tradition in southern China dating back over two thousand years — the ancient reservoir Anfeng Tang (安丰塘, also called Shao Bei) in Anhui was built around the 6th century BCE and remains partly in use today.

meanings: used in 閌閬|闶阆[kang1 lang2]

components.note: 门 (door, gate) — 闶 names a door.
亢 (kàng) is close to the sound of 闶 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 老屋的闶门已经破旧了。
example.pinyin: Lǎo wū de kāngmén yǐjīng pòjiù le.
example.english: The old house's door has become worn and shabby.
example.fact: 闶 is a rare literary character for a door or doorway, now essentially obsolete outside of classical texts and a handful of place names, having been fully displaced by the common word 门.

components.note: 门 (a door, an enclosure) suggests a container or box from which something is drawn.
龟 (tortoise) recalls the ancient Chinese practice of divination using tortoise shells; 阄 preserves that link to chance and the drawing of lots.

example.hanzi: 他们用抓阄的方式决定顺序。
example.pinyin: Tāmen yòng zhuā jiū de fāngshì juédìng shùnxù.
example.english: They decided the order by drawing lots.
example.fact: 抓阄 (zhuā jiū), 'to draw lots,' remains a common, fair way to make group decisions in China today, from splitting inherited property to assigning seats, tracing back to ancient methods of divination by chance.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, altar) — 祚 relates to blessing and the throne, matters bestowed by heaven.
乍 (zhà) no longer closely resembles 祚's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 百姓祈求上天赐福降祚。
example.pinyin: Bǎixìng qíqiú shàngtiān cì fú jiàng zuò.
example.english: The common people prayed for heaven to bestow blessings and fortune.
example.fact: 祚 appears in the classical term 国祚 (guózuò), 'the fortune/duration of a dynasty's rule,' a phrase historians still use today to discuss how long a given dynasty or regime lasted.

meanings: used in 鶻鵃|鹘鸼[gu3 zhou1]

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹘 names a falcon or pigeon-like bird.
骨 (gǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 鹘's reading.

example.hanzi: 鹘鸼是古书中记载的一种鸟。
example.pinyin: Gǔzhōu shì gǔshū zhōng jìzǎi de yì zhǒng niǎo.
example.english: The guzhou is a bird recorded in ancient texts.
example.fact: 鹘鸼 (gǔzhōu) is an old name, recorded in classical Chinese dictionaries, for a wood-pigeon-like bird — this gǔ reading is distinct from the far more common falcon-related reading hú, used in words like 鹰鹘 for swift birds of prey.
